Zaire. The Democratic Republic of the Congo underwent a dramatic renaming to Zaire in nineteen-seventy-one under dictator Mobutu Sese Seko as part of an Africanization campaign. The country reverted to Democratic Republic of the Congo in nineteen-ninety-seven after Mobutu's fall, reclaiming its original post-colonial name. The rebranding to Zaire, derived from a Bantu word for river, was meant to sever ties with European colonialism, though it became synonymous with decades of authoritarian rule and resource extraction.

The region's history under colonial rule was brutal. It was first the Congo Free State from eighteen-eighty-five to nineteen-oh-eight, personally ruled by Belgian King Leopold the Second, notorious for brutal exploitation and millions of deaths. Belgium then annexed the territory as the Belgian Congo from nineteen-oh-eight to nineteen-sixty, developing mining and infrastructure but maintaining colonial extraction. The nation gained independence in nineteen-sixty as the Democratic Republic of the Congo, also called Congo-Kinshasa to distinguish it from the Republic of the Congo.

Mobutu Sese Seko seized power in nineteen-sixty-five and consolidated authoritarian rule. In nineteen-seventy-one, he renamed the country Zaire, claiming to embrace indigenous African identity. The name Zaire derives from a Bantu word meaning river, referencing the mighty Congo River. But the name became tainted by association with Mobutu's kleptocratic regime and thirty-two years of plunder. After Mobutu's fall in nineteen-ninety-seven, Laurent-Désiré Kabila restored the original name Democratic Republic of the Congo, symbolically rejecting the authoritarian era and reconnecting the nation to its post-colonial identity.
